title: Tube Thoracostomy (Chest Tube)
keywords: insert above the rib not below
massive hemothorax 1500 mL initial or 200 mL per hour
re-expansion pulmonary edema large volume drainage
sources: ATLS 10th Edition — American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (chest tube technique, massive hemothorax criteria).
Kong VY, et al. A practical approach to tube thoracostomy. S Afr J Surg. 2019.
Laan DV, et al. Chest wall thickness and decompression failure: a systematic review. Injury. 2016 (landmark/depth considerations).
British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline 2010 (re-expansion pulmonary edema, drainage volume limits).

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (chest tube placement had no dedicated module). Sequential workflow: landmarks, blunt dissection technique, tube sizing, confirmation, massive-hemothorax/re-expansion-pulmonary-edema decision points.

purpose: A step-through for open (blunt-dissection) tube thoracostomy — landmarks, technique, tube sizing, and the decision points around massive hemothorax and re-expansion pulmonary edema — for bedside reference or pre-procedure rehearsal, not a substitute for supervised training on your first attempts.
entryPrompt: Confirm the indication and the landmark before you cut — most avoidable complications come from working outside the triangle of safety.

nodes.body: Indications: pneumothorax (after needle/finger decompression of a tension pneumothorax, or any significant/symptomatic simple pneumothorax), hemothorax, traumatic hemopneumothorax, empyema, malignant effusion. Landmark — the triangle of safety: bordered anteriorly by the lateral edge of pectoralis major, posteriorly by the lateral edge of latissimus dorsi, and inferiorly by a horizontal line at the nipple level (4th-5th intercostal space); apex toward the axilla. Position the patient supine or slightly head-up with the ipsilateral arm abducted or placed behind the head to open up the triangle.

Sterile prep and drape the field. Anesthetize generously with local anesthetic — skin, subcutaneous tissue, intercostal muscle, and the rib periosteum and parietal pleura itself (both are pain-sensitive; under-anesthetizing the pleura is the most common reason this procedure is remembered as agonizing). In an awake patient, this is also the moment to give IV analgesia/procedural sedation if the situation allows for it.

Make a 2-3 cm skin incision parallel to the rib, centered over the interspace one rib-space below your intended entry point, then dissect up and over the top of the rib below — this keeps you clear of the intercostal neurovascular bundle, which runs along the INFERIOR margin of each rib. Use a curved clamp (Kelly) for blunt dissection through subcutaneous tissue and intercostal muscle, staying on top of the lower rib the entire way.

Puncture the parietal pleura with the clamp in a controlled, deliberate motion (a rush of air or blood confirms you are in the pleural space), then spread the clamp to open a tract large enough for a finger. Perform a finger sweep: confirm you are in the free pleural space, clear any adhesions immediately around the tract, and confirm you do NOT feel abdominal organs, diaphragm, or a mass where lung should be — this is the single step that prevents the catastrophic misplacement of a chest tube into the abdomen.

Guide the tube into the pleural space with a clamp, directing it based on indication: posteriorly and superiorly (toward the apex) for a pneumothorax being drained of air; posteriorly and inferiorly (toward the base) for a hemothorax or effusion being drained of fluid. Advance until all drainage-tube side holes are well within the chest — confirmed by the tube's depth marking and by feeling no resistance. Tube size: 28-32 Fr for trauma/hemothorax (large bore needed to evacuate blood and clot without occluding); 20-24 Fr is adequate for a simple pneumothorax; a small-bore Seldinger pigtail catheter is an increasingly used, less painful alternative for a stable simple pneumothorax or effusion.

Connect immediately to a chest drainage/water-seal system (with suction only if directed, otherwise water seal alone). Confirm correct placement: fogging/condensation visible in the tube with respiration, respiratory swing at the water seal, immediate clinical improvement, and breath sounds returning. Secure with both a purse-string closure suture around the tube and a separate anchoring stitch, then an occlusive dressing. Obtain a chest X-ray to confirm tube position, resolution of the pneumothorax/hemothorax, and to rule out kinking or a fissure placement.

nodes.prompt: Two decision points that change management
nodes.body: Massive hemothorax → OR, not just a bigger tube: an initial chest-tube output of ≥ 1500 mL, OR ongoing output of ≥ 200 mL/hour for 2-4 consecutive hours, meets criteria for emergent thoracotomy — activate surgery immediately rather than watching the drain. Re-expansion pulmonary edema: rapidly draining a large-volume effusion or long-standing pneumothorax can trigger unilateral pulmonary edema; for a large chronic effusion, limit initial drainage to roughly 1-1.5 L and clamp/slow the rate if the patient develops cough, chest tightness, or hypoxia during drainage, then resume more gradually.

checklist: Indication and side confirmed before prepping
Entry point is within the triangle of safety, at or above the 5th intercostal space
Local anesthetic infiltrated down to and including rib periosteum and pleura
Dissection stayed on top of the rib below the interspace, never along its inferior margin
Finger sweep performed and confirmed free pleural space before the tube goes in
Tube directed apically for air, basally for fluid
Purse-string AND separate anchoring suture placed
CXR obtained to confirm position and re-check for pneumothorax/hemothorax resolution
Massive-hemothorax thresholds (≥1500 mL initial or ≥200 mL/hr) checked against output before assuming the tube alone will fix it
buildNote: workflow outputType, sequential. Deliberately does not restate broader trauma resuscitation (trauma-primary-survey, hemorrhagic-shock-mtp) or the eFAST pneumothorax/hemothorax scan itself (efast-exam) — this module is the hands-on tube-placement sequence plus the two decision points (massive hemothorax, re-expansion pulmonary edema) that most directly change management mid-procedure.
